name: Chinese Red
lede: Chinese red is an old trade name that has pointed at two different pigments: cinnabar from China, and a lead-chromate red made in Europe.

sections.title: Which red
sections.body:
Paterson defines Chinese red as a chrome red pigment, and also as an obsolete name for cinnabar [1]. He adds that Chinese vermilion is a vivid yellow-red pigment [1]. The two meanings are a classic case where books disagree about one name [1][2].

The cinnabar meaning is the older. Cinnabar was widely used by the Chinese from the third millennium BC and was formerly called Chinese red [3]. It is a vermilion color, close to [[vermilion]] and the redder end of [[scarlet]].

The chrome meaning came later. The Pigment Compendium records Heaton (1928) listing Chinese red as a synonym of chrome red, while Kuhn and Curran (1986) call it an older term for basic lead chromate and Schiek (1973) an older name for a chrome [[orange]] [2]. A long list of synonyms for chrome orange and red, among them American vermilion, Derby red, Victoria red and Vienna red, includes it too [2].

sections.title: China in a trade name
sections.body: The word China in a pigment name does not always mean the pigment came from there [1]. Paterson notes that Chinese blue is another name for Prussian blue, discovered in Berlin, and that Chinese white is zinc oxide, possibly named for fine porcelain [1]. Partridge, cited by Paterson, holds that Chinese white, orange and yellow all originated in China [1]. For the chrome meaning, the adjective looks like a trade label rather than a place of origin [1][2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: This red appears within six units of 410 of 23,781 paintings at five per cent of the canvas or more, about 1.7 per cent [4]. It was far more common in the 1400s, at 4.3 times the overall rate, with 70 of 945 paintings [4]. Albrecht Durer shows it in 7 of 47 works [4]. The strongest match is a 1440 Sienese panel of the Night Watchmen's salaries, at 52 per cent of its surface [4][[painting:rijks-20026322|Payment of Salaries to the Night Watchmen]]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a match is a color on a screen, not a pigment test [4].
